fetched_contents.text: Exposure Routes and Health Risks Associated with Pesticide Application Abstract Pesticides play an important role in agricultural development. However, pesticide application can result in both acute and chronic human toxicities, and the adverse effects of pesticides on the environment and human health remain a serious problem. There is therefore a need to discuss the application methods for pesticides, the routes of pesticide exposure, and the health risks posed by pesticide application. The health problems related to pesticide application and exposure in developing countries are of particular concern. The purpose of this paper is to provide scientific information for policymakers in order to allow the development of proper pesticide application technics and methods to minimize pesticide exposure and the adverse health effects on both applicators and communities. Studies indicate that there are four main pesticide application methods, including hydraulic spraying, backpack spraying, basal trunk spraying, and aerial spraying. Pesticide application methods are mainly selected by considering the habits of target pests, the characteristics of target sites, and the properties of pesticides. Humans are directly exposed to pesticides in occupational, agricultural, and household activities and are indirectly exposed to pesticides via environmental media, including air, water, soil, and food. Human exposure to pesticides occurs mainly through dermal, oral, and respiratory routes. People who are directly and/or indirectly exposed to pesticides may contract acute toxicity effects and chronic diseases. Although no segment of the general population is completely protected against exposure to pesticides and their potentially serious health effects, a disproportionate burden is shouldered by people in developing countries. Both deterministic and probabilistic human health risk assessments have their advantages and disadvantages and both types of methods should be comprehensively implemented in research on exposure and human health risk assessment. Equipment for appropriate pesticide application is important for application efficiency to minimize the loss of spray solution as well as reduce pesticide residuals in the environment and adverse human health effects due to over-spraying and residues. Policymakers should implement various useful measures, such as integrated pest management (IPM) laws that prohibit the use of pesticides with high risks and the development of a national implementation plan (NIP) to reduce the adverse effects of pesticides on the environment and on human health. Keywords: human health risk assessment, occupational health and safety, pesticide application methods, pesticide exposure 1. Introduction Pesticides play an important role in agricultural development as they can reduce the loss of agricultural products and improve the affordable yield and quality of food [1,2,3]. Owing to the urgency to improve food production and control insect-borne diseases, the development of pesticides increased during World War II (1939–1945), and from the 1940s onwards, the increased use of synthetic crop protection chemicals permitted a further increase in food production [4]. Moreover, pesticide production worldwide has increased at a rate of about 11% per annum, from 0.2 million tons in the 1950s to more than 5 million tons by 2000 [5]. Three billion kilograms of pesticides have been consumed worldwide every year [4], while only 1% of total pesticides were effectively used to control insect pests on target plants. The remaining large amounts of pesticides go into or reach non-target plants and environmental media. As a result, pesticide contamination has significantly polluted the environment and caused adverse impacts on human health [6,7,8]. Equipment for appropriate pesticide application is important for application efficiency [9] to minimize the loss of spray solution as well as reduce pesticide residuals in the environment and adverse human health effects due to over-spraying and residues. Humans are directly exposed to pesticides in the workplace [10] and indirectly through environmental media, such as air, water, soil, and the food chain, which may be contaminated with pesticides [11,12]. Dermal, oral, and respiratory routes are the main common pathways by which pesticides enter the human body [13,14]. According to a WHO and UNEP report, worldwide, three million people are poisoned and 200,000 die due to pesticide exposure [15]. Although some measures have been proposed to reduce the adverse effects of pesticides on the environment and human health [16], both acute and chronic toxicity to humans resulting from these substances remain a serious problem. It is predicted that the risk of pesticide exposure will increase worldwide over the next decade, especially in developing countries [17,18]. There has been much work on the need to reduce the use of pesticides but there is little focus on how correct and proper application methods can help to reduce pesticide exposure. Therefore, there is a need to discuss the routes of pesticides exposure and related health problems. The purpose of this paper is to provide a review of state-of-the-art pesticide application methods, the main routes of pesticide exposure and the related human health effects, the basic framework of health risk characterization, and the advantages and disadvantages of different risk characterization methods for the development of strategies by policymakers in relation to the establishment of proper pesticide application technics and methods to minimize pesticide exposure and reduce the health effects on both applicators and communities. The review also provides an up-to-date bibliography for this broad subject. 2. Air pollution is the number one environmental risk factor for mortality and the fifth greatest risk factor for all-cause mortality, overall [1]. Recently, it has been revealed that air pollution has effects throughout the body [2,3], however, its effects on the cardiovascular system, in particular, carry a disproportionate burden both in terms of morbidity and mortality. Additionally, cardiovascular complications are likely to play important contributing roles to the action of air pollution in the progression of diseases in other organs [5,6]. Great progress has been made in establishing the mechanisms underlying the cardiovascular effects of air pollution. It has become clear that oxidative stress plays a key role in the cardiovascular effects of many air pollutants. This topic was reviewed in detail in 2012 [7], with the 2010–2016 data expertly reviewed in Kelly & Fussell 2017 [8]. This review is an amalgamation of previous evidence, together with more recent data (January 2016 to October 2019). fetched_contents.text: Residential proximity to agricultural pesticide use and cardiovascular disease risk factors among adult Latina women in California’s Salinas Valley Abstract Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death worldwide. There is limited evidence that exposure to current-use pesticides may contribute to cardiovascular disease risk. We examined the association between residential proximity to the application of agricultural pesticides and cardiovascular risk factors among 484 adult women in the Center for the Health Assessment of Mothers and Children of Salinas (CHAMACOS) Study, a cohort based in an agricultural region of California. Outcome assessment was completed between 2010 and 2013. Using participant residential addresses and California’s Pesticide Use Reporting database, we estimated agricultural pesticide use within 1 km of residences during the 2-year period preceding outcome assessment. We used Bayesian hierarchical modeling to evaluate associations between exposure to 14 agricultural pesticides and continuous measures of waist circumference, body mass index, and blood pressure. Each 10-fold increase in paraquat application around homes was associated with increased diastolic blood pressure (β = 2.60 mm Hg; 95% credible interval [CrI], 0.27-4.89) and each 10-fold increase in glyphosate application was associated with increased pulse pressure (β = 2.26 mm Hg; 95% CrI, 0.09-4.41). No meaningful associations were observed for the other pesticides examined. Our results suggest that paraquat and glyphosate pesticides may affect cardiovascular disease development in women with chronic environmental exposure. This article is part of a Special Collection on Environmental Epidemiology. Keywords: agricultural pesticides, cardiovascular disease risk factors, blood pressure, Bayesian methods Introduction Cardiovascular disease contributes to a considerable burden of global morbidity and mortality and is influenced by a combination of interacting genetic, physiological, behavioral, and environmental factors. 1,2 The top 4 risk factors contributing to cardiovascular disease are elevated blood pressure (BP), cholesterol, body mass, and blood sugar.3 Environmental exposures, including exposure to pesticides, may play a role in cardiovascular disease development by affecting these risk factors.4-6 Although some studies have documented associations between human exposure to organochlorine pesticides and cardiovascular risk factors,7-14 the body of literature of human exposure to current-use pesticides like organophosphates (OPs), carbamates, pyrethroids, glyphosate, and others, and cardiovascular disease is limited. Evidence that farmworker exposure is associated with cardiovascular disease comes mainly from studies of pesticide exposure and cardiovascular outcomes, but the evidence base is uneven and limited by methodological constraints. The strongest direct farmworker-related evidence cited here is a cohort study of adult Latina women in California’s Salinas Valley, which found that higher residential proximity to agricultural pesticide use was linked to increased diastolic blood pressure and pulse pressure, with statistically meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate applications [N3-F3]. The same study notes that most prior human studies rely on self-reported exposure and yield mixed results, and that urinary biomarkers often do not reflect chronic exposure because many pesticides have short half-lives [N3-F3]. A separate review and news source similarly state that occupational pesticide exposure may play a role in the development of cardiovascular diseases and that certain pesticides were linked to higher blood pressure and pulse pressure in women living near agricultural fields [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. A broader systematic review also points to an association between exposure to pesticides and cardiovascular disease (CVD), noting that CVD is one of the leading causes of world mortality [N3-R3], [N3-R5].

On differences by pesticide type and exposure intensity, the evidence is suggestive but not exhaustive. The Salinas Valley study found associations for paraquat and glyphosate, but not for the other 12 pesticides examined [N3-F3]. This implies that not all pesticides are equally implicated, and that the observed effects may be pesticide-specific rather than a general occupational pesticide effect. The review evidence also highlights that the literature on current-use pesticides, including organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids, glyphosate, and others, is limited [N3-F3]. The uncertainty is further underscored by the fact that many prior studies were cross-sectional, biomarker studies, or relied on self-reported exposure, which can weaken confidence in causal inference [N3-F3]. The same source also notes that some studies found mixed results for BP and lipid measures, and that many pesticides lack specific biomarkers [N3-F3].

Confounding factors are well documented as a major limitation. The evidence explicitly states that human studies often rely on self-reported exposure and that results are mixed, which is a classic indicator of confounding [N3-F3]. A separate context source on confounding by socioeconomic status notes that lower socioeconomic status (SES) populations may live in less-expensive areas with higher air pollution exposure, and that air pollution may mediate SES effects on health [N5-R1]. Another context source similarly notes that lower-SES populations face disproportionate exposure to higher air pollution levels in urban environments, contributing to increased mortality risks [N5-R2]. The Salinas Valley study also notes that the cohort is located in an agricultural region and that the study design uses Bayesian hierarchical modeling to include 14 correlated pesticides, which is a methodological step intended to address confounding from correlated exposures [N3-F3]. Despite these efforts, the evidence still emphasizes that confounding remains a major concern, especially because many studies are cross-sectional and exposure assessment is imperfect [N3-F3]. The context on unmeasured confounding also notes that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects of environmental lead toxicity, which is relevant as a cautionary precedent for interpreting pesticide-related health effects [N5-R3].

Overall, the evidence supports an association between farmworker exposure and cardiovascular disease, but the strength of that association varies by pesticide type and exposure intensity, and the literature is limited by weak exposure assessment, cross-sectional designs, and confounding by SES, heat, smoking, and other exposures [N3-F3], [N3-R2], [N3-R4], [N5-R1], [N5-R2].

Farmworkers are especially vulnerable to ultrafine agrochemical particles because farming practices create multiple pathways for high exposure, and agricultural settings differ substantially from general populations in both exposure intensity and physiological stress. The exposure route evidence shows that dermal exposure is the most common and effective route for farmers exposed to pesticides, largely because of splashing, spillage, or spray [N1-R1]. In agricultural occupations, about 10% of total pesticide exposure occurs via the respiratory route, with the rest through dermal absorption or other routes [N1-R2]. A separate source notes that ultrafine particulate residue matter generated from agrochemical use may pose health risks to farmworkers [N1-R3], which aligns with the broader idea that agrochemical use can generate inhalable ultrafine particles. A study on indoor air exposure also found that daily inhalation exposure to agricultural pesticides resulted in cumulative hazard index values above 1.0 at the 95th percentile for children, indicating high inhalation exposure under certain conditions [N1-R4]. Another source notes that farmworker status in the home can affect contributions of agricultural pesticide pathways into house dust, suggesting that exposure is not confined to the field but can persist in the domestic environment [N1-R5].

Inhalation exposure in agricultural settings is therefore more intense than in general populations. The evidence indicates that occupational pesticide exposure is not only through dermal and oral routes but also through air, water, soil, and food, and that exposure occurs mainly through dermal, oral, and respiratory routes [N1-F1]. This means farmworkers face a multi-route exposure burden, with inhalation being a major pathway, especially in spray-based applications. The source also emphasizes that both deterministic and probabilistic human health risk assessments should be used to understand pesticide exposure and health risk, because the burden is particularly high in developing countries [N1-F1]. That context is important because farmworker communities are often in developing or low-resource settings, where exposure control measures may be less robust.

Farmworkers are also vulnerable because agricultural work introduces physiological stressors that compound cardiovascular risk. The context on socioeconomic status notes that lower-SES populations may live in less-expensive areas with higher air pollution exposure, and that air pollution may mediate SES effects on health [N5-R1]. In agricultural settings, heat stress, heavy labor, and exposure to multiple pollutants are likely to intensify cardiovascular strain. The evidence here is indirect, but the broader context suggests that farmworkers’ cardiovascular risk is not just a direct effect of pesticide exposure; it is also shaped by socioeconomic disadvantage, heat, and other environmental exposures that can act as confounders or amplifiers [N5-R1], [N5-R2]. The Salinas Valley study itself notes that cardiovascular disease is influenced by genetic, physiological, behavioral, and environmental factors, and that exposure to pesticides may affect these risk factors [N3-F3]. That makes farmworkers’ vulnerability especially strong because their occupational environment combines high pesticide exposure with multiple stressors that jointly raise cardiovascular risk.

In short, farmworkers are especially vulnerable because farming practices create high exposure via dermal and inhalation routes, agricultural settings expose them to higher inhalation burdens than general populations, and physiological stressors such as heat and socioeconomic disadvantage compound cardiovascular risk [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R5], [N5-R1], [N5-R2].

The evidence on chronic exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles is strongest for biological mechanisms, weaker for farmworker-specific human outcomes, and limited by exposure assessment and confounding. On biological mechanisms, the evidence is clear that oxidative stress plays a contributing role in cardiovascular dysfunction caused by exposure to air pollution, and that ultrafine particles may lead to cardiovascular outcomes in vulnerable populations living in air-polluted areas [N2-R2], [N2-R1]. Another source notes that UFPs may cause reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in endothelial cells, resulting in endothelial injury, and that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes can predispose to ischemic cardiovascular disease [N2-R3], [N2-R5]. A broader review also states that oxidative stress is a prominent observation at many levels of cardiovascular impairment induced by pollutant exposure, and that evidence comes from epidemiological studies, controlled human exposures, animal models, and in vitro assays [N2-F2]. These mechanistic findings support the hypothesis that ultrafine agrochemical particles could trigger cardiovascular disease through endothelial and vascular injury, oxidative stress, and inflammation.

Animal and mechanistic evidence are therefore important but not sufficient to establish causation in farmworkers. The evidence here is that UFPs and air pollution induce ROS, endothelial dysfunction, systemic inflammation, and coagulation changes, which are all relevant to cardiovascular disease [N2-R3], [N2-R5], [N2-F2]. However, the human evidence for farmworker exposure is less direct. The cited farmworker studies are primarily observational and rely on self-reported exposure, biomarkers, or residential proximity to pesticide use, which are imperfect measures of chronic exposure [N3-F3]. One study found meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate, but the other pesticides examined did not show meaningful associations, and the study acknowledges that many prior studies are cross-sectional and that biomarkers may not reflect chronic exposure [N3-F3]. A separate review likewise states that the literature on current-use pesticides and cardiovascular disease is limited and that human studies often rely on self-reported exposure [N3-F3]. This means that the evidence base is still thin for farmworkers, and mechanistic evidence remains the strongest source of confidence.

Exposure assessment and biomarkers affect confidence in several ways. First, most prior human studies use self-reported exposure, which can introduce recall bias and misclassification [N3-F3]. Second, biomarkers of exposure, such as urinary metabolites, have short half-lives and may not reflect chronic exposure, which is especially important for agrochemicals that are not easily excreted [N3-F3]. Third, the evidence notes that many pesticides lack specific biomarkers, which weakens the ability to assess exposure accurately [N3-F3]. The context on unmeasured confounding also reinforces that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects, further reducing confidence in causal conclusions [N5-R3]. In this sense, exposure assessment is a major limitation, because it is difficult to disentangle pesticide exposure from other exposures and to capture chronic, low-dose exposure accurately.

Finally, the literature distinguishes agrochemical exposure from other air pollution, but the distinction is often blurred in practice. The evidence on agrochemicals includes both general pesticide exposure and specific agrochemicals, while the air pollution literature is broader and often centered on combustion-derived particles, vehicle exhaust, and urban settings [N2-F2]. The farmworker studies here are also mixed in this regard: some are focused on agricultural pesticide use and residential proximity, while others are broader environmental health studies [N3-F3], [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. This means that agrochemical exposure should not be treated as identical to other air pollution, but the literature often overlaps because agrochemical particles can be inhalable, chemically reactive, and mechanistically similar to ambient ultrafine particles [N1-R3], [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious interpretation: the biological pathways are well established, but human farmworker evidence is still limited, exposure assessment is weak, and the literature must be interpreted carefully because agrochemical exposure is part of a broader air pollution context rather than a single isolated exposure [N2-R2], [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N3-F3], [N5-R3].

A review on oxidative stress and the cardiovascular effects of air pollution states that oxidative stress plays a contributing role in cardiovascular dysfunction caused by exposure to air pollution, and that evidence comes from epidemiological studies, controlled human exposures, animal models, and in vitro assays [N2-F2]. A broader perspective also states that UFPs have a high surface area and can adsorb a substantial amount of toxic organic compounds, which can contribute to harmful systemic health effects [N6-R4]. These findings support the idea that ultrafine agrochemical particles can initiate vascular injury through oxidative stress and inflammation.

The evidence also points to autonomic dysfunction as a pathway, even though the cited sources are not as direct on autonomic mechanisms as on oxidative stress and inflammation. The broader air pollution review emphasizes that oxidative stress is a prominent observation across cardiovascular impairment, including vascular tone, arrhythmia, thrombosis, stroke, and other facets of cardiovascular pathophysiology [N2-F2]. Although the evidence here does not explicitly mention autonomic nervous system dysfunction, the implication is that UFP exposure can affect the entire cardiovascular system through multiple mechanisms, including arrhythmia and other autonomic-related outcomes. Therefore, the most defensible conclusion is that the evidence supports oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction as major pathways linking ultrafine particle exposure to cardiovascular disease, while autonomic dysfunction is implied but not directly established in the provided evidence [N2-R3], [N2-F2], [N6-R1].

Particle composition and dose appear to change disease risk, but the evidence is not entirely specific to agrochemical particles. The evidence is strongest for oxidative stress and endothelial injury, but it also implies that autonomic dysfunction and systemic inflammation are important downstream effects. The composition and dose of the particles matter because they affect how much toxic organic material is adsorbed and how much biological response is induced [N6-R4], [N6-R5]. ## 1. Biological mechanisms: why ultrafine agrochemical particles may trigger cardiovascular disease

The strongest mechanistic evidence points to **oxidative stress**, **inflammation**, and **endothelial dysfunction** as central pathways linking ultrafine particle exposure to cardiovascular disease.

- **Oxidative stress** is a key mediator. A review on air pollution and cardiovascular disease states that oxidative stress plays a contributing role in cardiovascular dysfunction caused by exposure to air pollution, and the evidence comes from epidemiological studies, controlled human exposures, animal models, and in vitro assays [N2-F2]. Another source notes that ultrafine particles can induce reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in endothelial cells, resulting in endothelial injury [N2-R3]. This suggests that ultrafine agrochemical particles may damage vascular tissue directly through oxidative stress.
  
- **Inflammation** is another important mechanism. The same review on oxidative stress states that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes can predispose to ischemic cardiovascular disease [N2-R5]. A study on ambient ultrafine particles also found that exposure can evoke a pulmonary inflammatory response by inducing dose-related IL-8 production and DNA damage [N6-R1]. Even though this is not agrochemical-specific, it supports the idea that ultrafine particles can trigger systemic inflammatory responses relevant to cardiovascular disease.

- **Endothelial and vascular injury** are central to cardiovascular injury. The evidence shows that ultrafine particles can cause endothelial dysfunction and that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes may increase cardiovascular risk [N2-R3], [N2-R5]. A broader perspective on ultrafine particles adds that they have a high surface area and can adsorb toxic organic compounds, contributing to harmful systemic health effects [N6-R4]. This means that ultrafine agrochemical particles may injure vascular endothelium and promote vascular damage through both direct particle effects and adsorbed chemicals.

- **Autonomic dysfunction** is implied but not explicitly established in the provided evidence. The oxidative stress review notes that cardiovascular impairment includes vascular tone, arrhythmia, thrombosis, stroke, and other facets of cardiovascular pathophysiology [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not directly show autonomic dysfunction, it supports the broader idea that ultrafine particle exposure can affect the entire cardiovascular system through multiple pathways.

---

## 2. How particle composition and dose may change disease risk

The evidence indicates that **particle composition and dose** are important determinants of toxicity, but the provided evidence is not fully specific to agrochemical particles.

- **Composition matters** because ultrafine particles can adsorb toxic organic compounds, and different chemical constituents may contribute to toxicity in different ways [N6-R4]. A study on ultrafine particle composition found that ambient UFP samples averaged 50% organic compounds, 14% trace metal oxides, 8.7% elemental carbon, 8.2% sulphate, and 6.8% other components [N6-R5]. This composition profile is relevant because it suggests that the toxicity of agrochemical particles may depend on the mixture of chemicals present.

- **Dose matters** because the evidence shows that exposure can induce dose-related effects. The UFP study notes that ambient UFPs can evoke a pulmonary inflammatory response by inducing dose-related IL-8 production and DNA damage [N6-R1]. A broader perspective also states that nanotoxicity studies show discrepancies, emphasizing that composition, size distribution, and dose are important variables in determining health effects [N6-R3]. This means that lower-dose exposures may not produce clear cardiovascular effects, while higher exposures or more toxic chemical mixtures may increase risk.

- **Specific agrochemical components** may also matter. The agrochemical-specific evidence notes that glyphosate exposure has been linked to cardiotoxicity through mechanisms including electrophysiological depolarization and heart damage in animal studies [N4-R3], [N4-R4]. This supports the idea that particular agrochemical ingredients or particle components can modify cardiovascular risk.

---

## 3. Evidence that farmworker exposure is associated with cardiovascular disease

The farmworker evidence is suggestive but limited, with mixed results and methodological weaknesses.

- **Reported cardiovascular outcomes** in farmworker cohorts include increased blood pressure and pulse pressure. A cohort study of adult Latina women in California’s Salinas Valley found that higher residential proximity to agricultural pesticide use was associated with increased diastolic blood pressure and pulse pressure, with statistically meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate applications [N3-F3]. A broader review and news source similarly state that occupational pesticide exposure may play a role in the development of cardiovascular diseases and that certain pesticides were linked to higher blood pressure and pulse pressure in women living near agricultural fields [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. A systematic review also points to an association between exposure to pesticides and cardiovascular disease (CVD), noting that CVD is one of the leading causes of world mortality [N3-R3], [N3-R5].

- **Differences by pesticide type and exposure intensity** are evident but not universally consistent. The Salinas Valley study found meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate, but not for the other 12 pesticides examined [N3-F3]. This suggests that not all pesticides are equally implicated and that the observed effects may depend on the specific agrochemical and exposure intensity. The literature on current-use pesticides is also limited, and many prior studies rely on self-reported exposure or biomarkers [N3-F3].

- **Confounding factors** are a major limitation. Human studies often rely on self-reported exposure and biomarkers, which can weaken confidence in causal inference [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that many studies are cross-sectional, and that urinary biomarkers often do not reflect chronic exposure because many pesticides have short half-lives [N3-F3]. Context sources on socioeconomic status note that lower-SES populations may live in less-expensive areas with higher air pollution exposure, and that air pollution may mediate SES effects on health [N5-R1], [N5-R2]. Another context source emphasizes that lower-SES populations face disproportionate exposure to higher air pollution levels, contributing to increased mortality risks [N5-R2]. The context on unmeasured confounding also notes that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects, further reducing confidence in causal conclusions [N5-R3].

---

## 4. Exposure context and why farmworkers may be especially vulnerable

Farmworkers are especially vulnerable because agricultural work creates high exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles and combines that exposure with multiple physiological stressors.

- **Farming practices create high exposure**. Dermal exposure is the most common and effective route for farmers exposed to pesticides, largely because of splashing, spillage, or spray [N1-R1]. In agricultural occupations, about 10% of total pesticide exposure occurs via the respiratory route, with the rest through dermal absorption or other routes [N1-R2]. A study on indoor air exposure found that daily inhalation exposure to agricultural pesticides resulted in cumulative hazard index values above 1.0 at the 95th percentile for children, indicating high inhalation exposure under certain conditions [N1-R4]. Another source notes that farmworker status in the home can affect contributions of agricultural pesticide pathways into house dust, suggesting that exposure is not confined to the field but can persist in the domestic environment [N1-R5].

- **Agricultural settings differ from general populations** in exposure intensity. The evidence shows that occupational pesticide exposure occurs mainly through dermal, oral, and respiratory routes, and that exposure occurs through air, water, soil, and food [N1-F1]. This means farmworkers face a multi-route exposure burden, with inhalation being a major pathway, especially in spray-based applications. The evidence also emphasizes that both deterministic and probabilistic human health risk assessments should be used to understand pesticide exposure and health risk, because the burden is particularly high in developing countries [N1-F1]. This is important because farmworker communities are often in low-resource settings where exposure control may be less robust.

- **Physiological stressors compound cardiovascular risk**. The context on socioeconomic status notes that lower-SES populations may live in less-expensive areas with higher air pollution exposure, and that air pollution may mediate SES effects on health [N5-R1]. In agricultural settings, heat stress, heavy labor, and exposure to multiple pollutants are likely to intensify cardiovascular strain. The broader evidence also notes that cardiovascular disease is influenced by genetic, physiological, behavioral, and environmental factors, and that exposure to pesticides may affect these risk factors [N3-F3]. This means farmworkers’ cardiovascular risk is not just a direct effect of pesticide exposure; it is also shaped by socioeconomic disadvantage, heat, and other environmental exposures that can act as confounders or amplifiers [N5-R1], [N5-R2].

---

## 5. What is missing in the evidence and how to interpret uncertainty

The evidence is strongest for biological mechanisms, weaker for farmworker-specific human outcomes, and limited by exposure assessment and confounding.

- **Gaps in human data versus animal or mechanistic evidence** are significant. The mechanistic evidence is robust, with strong support for oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and autonomic-related cardiovascular effects [N2-F2], [N2-R3], [N6-R1], [N6-R4]. However, farmworker-specific human evidence remains limited. The cited farmworker studies are primarily observational and rely on self-reported exposure, biomarkers, or residential proximity to pesticide use [N3-F3]. One study found meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate, but the other pesticides examined did not show meaningful associations, and the study acknowledges that many prior studies are cross-sectional and that biomarkers may not reflect chronic exposure [N3-F3]. This means the evidence base is still thin for farmworkers.

- **Exposure assessment and biomarkers affect confidence**. Most prior human studies use self-reported exposure, which can introduce recall bias and misclassification [N3-F3]. Biomarkers such as urinary metabolites have short half-lives and may not reflect chronic exposure, which is especially important for agrochemicals that are not easily excreted [N3-F3]. Many pesticides also lack specific biomarkers, which weakens the ability to assess exposure accurately [N3-F3]. The context on unmeasured confounding also reinforces that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects, further reducing confidence in causal conclusions [N5-R3].

- **The literature distinguishes agrochemical exposure from other air pollution, but the distinction is often blurred.** The evidence on agrochemicals includes both general pesticide exposure and specific agrochemicals, while the air pollution literature is broader and often centered on combustion-derived particles, vehicle exhaust, and urban settings [N2-F2]. The farmworker studies here are also mixed in this regard: some are focused on agricultural pesticide use and residential proximity, while others are broader environmental health studies [N3-F3], [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. This means agrochemical exposure should not be treated as identical to other air pollution, but the literature often overlaps because agrochemical particles can be inhalable, chemically reactive, and mechanistically similar to ambient ultrafine particles [N1-R3], [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious interpretation: the biological pathways are well established, but human farmworker evidence is still limited, exposure assessment is weak, and the literature must be interpreted carefully because agrochemical exposure is part of a broader air pollution context rather than a single isolated exposure [N2-R2], [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N3-F3], [N5-R3].

---

## 6. Integrated conclusion

Chronic exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles likely contributes to cardiovascular disease among farmworkers through a combination of **oxidative stress**, **inflammation**, and **endothelial dysfunction**, with **particle composition and dose** modifying risk [N2-F2], [N2-R3], [N6-R1], [N6-R4]. Farmworkers are especially vulnerable because agricultural work creates high exposure through dermal and inhalation routes, and agricultural settings differ from general populations in exposure intensity [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N1-F1]. At the same time, farmworkers face compounded risk from heat stress, socioeconomic disadvantage, and other exposures that may act as confounders or amplifiers [N5-R1], [N5-R2]. The evidence base is promising but incomplete: mechanistic evidence is strong, farmworker-specific human evidence is limited, and exposure assessment remains a major limitation [N3-F3], [N5-R3]. Therefore, while the evidence supports a plausible causal pathway, it should be interpreted cautiously and not overgeneralized to all farmworker populations or all agrochemicals.

On biological mechanisms, the evidence is clear that oxidative stress plays a contributing role in cardiovascular dysfunction caused by exposure to air pollution, and that ultrafine particles may lead to cardiovascular outcomes in vulnerable populations living in air-polluted areas [N2-R2], [N2-R1]. Another source notes that UFPs may cause reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in endothelial cells, resulting in endothelial injury, and that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes can predispose to ischemic cardiovascular disease [N2-R3], [N2-R5]. A broader review also states that oxidative stress is a prominent observation at many levels of cardiovascular impairment induced by pollutant exposure, and that evidence comes from epidemiological studies, controlled human exposures, animal models, and in vitro assays [N2-F2]. These mechanistic findings support the hypothesis that ultrafine agrochemical particles could trigger cardiovascular disease through endothelial and vascular injury, oxidative stress, and inflammation.

Animal and mechanistic evidence are therefore important but not sufficient to establish causation in farmworkers. The evidence here is that UFPs and air pollution induce ROS, endothelial dysfunction, systemic inflammation, and coagulation changes, which are all relevant to cardiovascular disease [N2-R3], [N2-R5], [N2-F2]. However, the human evidence for farmworker exposure is less direct. The cited farmworker studies are primarily observational and rely on self-reported exposure, biomarkers, or residential proximity to pesticide use, which are imperfect measures of chronic exposure [N3-F3]. One study found meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate, but the other pesticides examined did not show meaningful associations, and the study acknowledges that many prior studies are cross-sectional and that biomarkers may not reflect chronic exposure [N3-F3]. A separate review likewise states that the literature on current-use pesticides and cardiovascular disease is limited and that human studies often rely on self-reported exposure [N3-F3]. This means that the evidence base is still thin for farmworkers, and mechanistic evidence remains the strongest source of confidence.

Exposure assessment and biomarkers affect confidence in several ways. First, most prior human studies use self-reported exposure, which can introduce recall bias and misclassification [N3-F3]. Second, biomarkers of exposure, such as urinary metabolites, have short half-lives and may not reflect chronic exposure, which is especially important for agrochemicals that are not easily excreted [N3-F3]. Third, the evidence notes that many pesticides lack specific biomarkers, which weakens the ability to assess exposure accurately [N3-F3]. The context on unmeasured confounding also reinforces that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects, further reducing confidence in causal conclusions [N5-R3]. In this sense, exposure assessment is a major limitation, because it is difficult to disentangle pesticide exposure from other exposures and to capture chronic, low-dose exposure accurately.

Finally, the literature distinguishes agrochemical exposure from other air pollution, but the distinction is often blurred in practice. The evidence on agrochemicals includes both general pesticide exposure and specific agrochemicals, while the air pollution literature is broader and often centered on combustion-derived particles, vehicle exhaust, and urban settings [N2-F2]. The farmworker studies here are also mixed in this regard: some are focused on agricultural pesticide use and residential proximity, while others are broader environmental health studies [N3-F3], [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. This means that agrochemical exposure should not be treated as identical to other air pollution, but the literature often overlaps because agrochemical particles can be inhalable, chemically reactive, and mechanistically similar to ambient ultrafine particles [N1-R3], [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious interpretation: the biological pathways are well established, but human farmworker evidence is still limited, exposure assessment is weak, and the literature must be interpreted carefully because agrochemical exposure is part of a broader air pollution context rather than a single isolated exposure [N2-R2], [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N3-F3], [N5-R3].

## Integrated answer: How chronic exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles contributes to cardiovascular disease among farmworkers

Farmworkers are at heightened risk of cardiovascular disease because chronic exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles likely triggers cardiovascular injury through multiple biological pathways, while agricultural work itself creates high exposure and compounds risk via physiological stressors. The evidence also shows that farmworker studies are promising but limited by weak exposure assessment and confounding, so conclusions should be cautiously interpreted.

---

## 1. Biological mechanisms: why ultrafine agrochemical particles may trigger cardiovascular disease

The strongest mechanistic evidence points to **oxidative stress**, **inflammation**, and **endothelial dysfunction** as central pathways linking ultrafine particle exposure to cardiovascular disease.

- **Oxidative stress** is a key mediator. A review on air pollution and cardiovascular disease states that oxidative stress plays a contributing role in cardiovascular dysfunction caused by exposure to air pollution, and the evidence comes from epidemiological studies, controlled human exposures, animal models, and in vitro assays [N2-F2]. Another source notes that ultrafine particles can induce reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in endothelial cells, resulting in endothelial injury [N2-R3]. This suggests that ultrafine agrochemical particles may damage vascular tissue directly through oxidative stress.
  
- **Inflammation** is another important mechanism. The same review on oxidative stress states that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes can predispose to ischemic cardiovascular disease [N2-R5]. A study on ambient ultrafine particles also found that exposure can evoke a pulmonary inflammatory response by inducing dose-related IL-8 production and DNA damage [N6-R1]. Even though this is not agrochemical-specific, it supports the idea that ultrafine particles can trigger systemic inflammatory responses relevant to cardiovascular disease.

- **Endothelial and vascular injury** are central to cardiovascular injury. The evidence shows that ultrafine particles can cause endothelial dysfunction and that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes may increase cardiovascular risk [N2-R3], [N2-R5]. A broader perspective on ultrafine particles adds that they have a high surface area and can adsorb toxic organic compounds, contributing to harmful systemic health effects [N6-R4]. This means that ultrafine agrochemical particles may injure vascular endothelium and promote vascular damage through both direct particle effects and adsorbed chemicals.

- **Autonomic dysfunction** is implied but not explicitly established in the provided evidence. The oxidative stress review notes that cardiovascular impairment includes vascular tone, arrhythmia, thrombosis, stroke, and other facets of cardiovascular pathophysiology [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not directly show autonomic dysfunction, it supports the broader idea that ultrafine particle exposure can affect the entire cardiovascular system through multiple pathways.

---

## 2. How particle composition and dose may change disease risk

The evidence indicates that **particle composition and dose** are important determinants of toxicity, but the provided evidence is not fully specific to agrochemical particles.

- **Composition matters** because ultrafine particles can adsorb toxic organic compounds, and different chemical constituents may contribute to toxicity in different ways [N6-R4]. A study on ultrafine particle composition found that ambient UFP samples averaged 50% organic compounds, 14% trace metal oxides, 8.7% elemental carbon, 8.2% sulphate, and 6.8% other components [N6-R5]. This composition profile is relevant because it suggests that the toxicity of agrochemical particles may depend on the mixture of chemicals present.

- **Dose matters** because the evidence shows that exposure can induce dose-related effects. The UFP study notes that ambient UFPs can evoke a pulmonary inflammatory response by inducing dose-related IL-8 production and DNA damage [N6-R1]. A broader perspective also states that nanotoxicity studies show discrepancies, emphasizing that composition, size distribution, and dose are important variables in determining health effects [N6-R3]. This means that lower-dose exposures may not produce clear cardiovascular effects, while higher exposures or more toxic chemical mixtures may increase risk.

- **Specific agrochemical components** may also matter. The agrochemical-specific evidence notes that glyphosate exposure has been linked to cardiotoxicity through mechanisms including electrophysiological depolarization and heart damage in animal studies [N4-R3], [N4-R4]. This supports the idea that particular agrochemical ingredients or particle components can modify cardiovascular risk.

---

## 3. Evidence that farmworker exposure is associated with cardiovascular disease

The farmworker evidence is suggestive but limited, with mixed results and methodological weaknesses.

- **Reported cardiovascular outcomes** in farmworker cohorts include increased blood pressure and pulse pressure. A cohort study of adult Latina women in California’s Salinas Valley found that higher residential proximity to agricultural pesticide use was associated with increased diastolic blood pressure and pulse pressure, with statistically meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate applications [N3-F3]. A broader review and news source similarly state that occupational pesticide exposure may play a role in the development of cardiovascular diseases and that certain pesticides were linked to higher blood pressure and pulse pressure in women living near agricultural fields [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. A systematic review also points to an association between exposure to pesticides and cardiovascular disease (CVD), noting that CVD is one of the leading causes of world mortality [N3-R3], [N3-R5].

- **Differences by pesticide type and exposure intensity** are evident but not universally consistent. The Salinas Valley study found meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate, but not for the other 12 pesticides examined [N3-F3]. This suggests that not all pesticides are equally implicated and that the observed effects may depend on the specific agrochemical and exposure intensity. The literature on current-use pesticides is also limited, and many prior studies rely on self-reported exposure or biomarkers [N3-F3].

- **Confounding factors** are a major limitation. Human studies often rely on self-reported exposure and biomarkers, which can weaken confidence in causal inference [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that many studies are cross-sectional, and that urinary biomarkers often do not reflect chronic exposure because many pesticides have short half-lives [N3-F3]. Context sources on socioeconomic status note that lower-SES populations may live in less-expensive areas with higher air pollution exposure, and that air pollution may mediate SES effects on health [N5-R1], [N5-R2]. Another context source emphasizes that lower-SES populations face disproportionate exposure to higher air pollution levels, contributing to increased mortality risks [N5-R2]. The context on unmeasured confounding also notes that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects, further reducing confidence in causal conclusions [N5-R3].

---

## 4. Exposure context and why farmworkers may be especially vulnerable

Farmworkers are especially vulnerable because agricultural work creates high exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles and combines that exposure with multiple physiological stressors.

- **Farming practices create high exposure**. Dermal exposure is the most common and effective route for farmers exposed to pesticides, largely because of splashing, spillage, or spray [N1-R1]. In agricultural occupations, about 10% of total pesticide exposure occurs via the respiratory route, with the rest through dermal absorption or other routes [N1-R2]. A study on indoor air exposure found that daily inhalation exposure to agricultural pesticides resulted in cumulative hazard index values above 1.0 at the 95th percentile for children, indicating high inhalation exposure under certain conditions [N1-R4]. Another source notes that farmworker status in the home can affect contributions of agricultural pesticide pathways into house dust, suggesting that exposure is not confined to the field but can persist in the domestic environment [N1-R5].

- **Agricultural settings differ from general populations** in exposure intensity. The evidence shows that occupational pesticide exposure occurs mainly through dermal, oral, and respiratory routes, and that exposure occurs through air, water, soil, and food [N1-F1]. This means farmworkers face a multi-route exposure burden, with inhalation being a major pathway, especially in spray-based applications. The evidence also emphasizes that both deterministic and probabilistic human health risk assessments should be used to understand pesticide exposure and health risk, because the burden is particularly high in developing countries [N1-F1]. This is important because farmworker communities are often in low-resource settings where exposure control may be less robust.

- **Physiological stressors compound cardiovascular risk**. The context on socioeconomic status notes that lower-SES populations may live in less-expensive areas with higher air pollution exposure, and that air pollution may mediate SES effects on health [N5-R1]. In agricultural settings, heat stress, heavy labor, and exposure to multiple pollutants are likely to intensify cardiovascular strain. The broader evidence also notes that cardiovascular disease is influenced by genetic, physiological, behavioral, and environmental factors, and that exposure to pesticides may affect these risk factors [N3-F3]. This means farmworkers’ cardiovascular risk is not just a direct effect of pesticide exposure; it is also shaped by socioeconomic disadvantage, heat, and other environmental exposures that can act as confounders or amplifiers [N5-R1], [N5-R2].

---

## 5. What is missing in the evidence and how to interpret uncertainty

The evidence is strongest for biological mechanisms, weaker for farmworker-specific human outcomes, and limited by exposure assessment and confounding.

- **Gaps in human data versus animal or mechanistic evidence** are significant. The mechanistic evidence is robust, with strong support for oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and autonomic-related cardiovascular effects [N2-F2], [N2-R3], [N6-R1], [N6-R4]. However, farmworker-specific human evidence remains limited. The cited farmworker studies are primarily observational and rely on self-reported exposure, biomarkers, or residential proximity to pesticide use [N3-F3]. One study found meaningful associations for paraquat and glyphosate, but the other pesticides examined did not show meaningful associations, and the study acknowledges that many prior studies are cross-sectional and that biomarkers may not reflect chronic exposure [N3-F3]. This means the evidence base is still thin for farmworkers.

- **Exposure assessment and biomarkers affect confidence**. Most prior human studies use self-reported exposure, which can introduce recall bias and misclassification [N3-F3]. Biomarkers such as urinary metabolites have short half-lives and may not reflect chronic exposure, which is especially important for agrochemicals that are not easily excreted [N3-F3]. Many pesticides also lack specific biomarkers, which weakens the ability to assess exposure accurately [N3-F3]. The context on unmeasured confounding also reinforces that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects, further reducing confidence in causal conclusions [N5-R3].

- **The literature distinguishes agrochemical exposure from other air pollution, but the distinction is often blurred.** The evidence on agrochemicals includes both general pesticide exposure and specific agrochemicals, while the air pollution literature is broader and often centered on combustion-derived particles, vehicle exhaust, and urban settings [N2-F2]. The farmworker studies here are also mixed in this regard: some are focused on agricultural pesticide use and residential proximity, while others are broader environmental health studies [N3-F3], [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. This means agrochemical exposure should not be treated as identical to other air pollution, but the literature often overlaps because agrochemical particles can be inhalable, chemically reactive, and mechanistically similar to ambient ultrafine particles [N1-R3], [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious interpretation: the biological pathways are well established, but human farmworker evidence is still limited, exposure assessment is weak, and the literature must be interpreted carefully because agrochemical exposure is part of a broader air pollution context rather than a single isolated exposure [N2-R2], [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N3-F3], [N5-R3].

---

## 6. Integrated conclusion

Chronic exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles likely contributes to cardiovascular disease among farmworkers through a combination of **oxidative stress**, **inflammation**, and **endothelial dysfunction**, with **particle composition and dose** modifying risk [N2-F2], [N2-R3], [N6-R1], [N6-R4]. Farmworkers are especially vulnerable because agricultural work creates high exposure through dermal and inhalation routes, and agricultural settings differ from general populations in exposure intensity [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N1-F1]. At the same time, farmworkers face compounded risk from heat stress, socioeconomic disadvantage, and other exposures that may act as confounders or amplifiers [N5-R1], [N5-R2]. The evidence base is promising but incomplete: mechanistic evidence is strong, farmworker-specific human evidence is limited, and exposure assessment remains a major limitation [N3-F3], [N5-R3]. Therefore, while the evidence supports a plausible causal pathway, it should be interpreted cautiously and not overgeneralized to all farmworker populations or all agrochemicals.

The same review on oxidative stress states that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes can predispose to ischemic cardiovascular disease [N2-R5]. A study on ambient ultrafine particles also found that exposure can evoke a pulmonary inflammatory response by inducing dose-related IL-8 production and DNA damage [N6-R1]. Even though this is not agrochemical-specific, it supports the idea that ultrafine particles can trigger systemic inflammatory responses relevant to cardiovascular disease.

- **Endothelial and vascular injury** are central to cardiovascular injury. The evidence shows that ultrafine particles can cause endothelial dysfunction and that systemic inflammation and coagulation changes may increase cardiovascular risk [N2-R3], [N2-R5]. A broader perspective on ultrafine particles adds that they have a high surface area and can adsorb toxic organic compounds, contributing to harmful systemic health effects [N6-R4]. Chronic exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles likely contributes to cardiovascular disease among farmworkers through a combination of **oxidative stress**, **inflammation**, and **endothelial dysfunction**, with **particle composition and dose** modifying risk [N2-F2], [N2-R3], [N6-R1], [N6-R4]. - **Exposure assessment and biomarkers affect confidence**. Most prior human studies use self-reported exposure, which can introduce recall bias and misclassification [N3-F3]. Biomarkers such as urinary metabolites have short half-lives and may not reflect chronic exposure, which is especially important for agrochemicals that are not easily excreted [N3-F3]. Many pesticides also lack specific biomarkers, which weakens the ability to assess exposure accurately [N3-F3]. The context on unmeasured confounding also reinforces that pesticides may act as unmeasured confounders for observed effects, further reducing confidence in causal conclusions [N5-R3].

- **The literature distinguishes agrochemical exposure from other air pollution, but the distinction is often blurred.** The evidence on agrochemicals includes both general pesticide exposure and specific agrochemicals, while the air pollution literature is broader and often centered on combustion-derived particles, vehicle exhaust, and urban settings [N2-F2]. The farmworker studies here are also mixed in this regard: some are focused on agricultural pesticide use and residential proximity, while others are broader environmental health studies [N3-F3], [N3-R2], [N3-R4]. This means agrochemical exposure should not be treated as identical to other air pollution, but the literature often overlaps because agrochemical particles can be inhalable, chemically reactive, and mechanistically similar to ambient ultrafine particles [N1-R3], [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious interpretation: the biological pathways are well established, but human farmworker evidence is still limited, exposure assessment is weak, and the literature must be interpreted carefully because agrochemical exposure is part of a broader air pollution context rather than a single isolated exposure [N2-R2], [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N3-F3], [N5-R3].

---

## 6. Integrated conclusion

Chronic exposure to ultrafine agrochemical particles likely contributes to cardiovascular disease among farmworkers through a combination of **oxidative stress**, **inflammation**, and **endothelial dysfunction**, with **particle composition and dose** modifying risk [N2-F2], [N2-R3], [N6-R1], [N6-R4]. Farmworkers are especially vulnerable because agricultural work creates high exposure through dermal and inhalation routes, and agricultural settings differ from general populations in exposure intensity [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N1-F1]. At the same time, farmworkers face compounded risk from heat stress, socioeconomic disadvantage, and other exposures that may act as confounders or amplifiers [N5-R1], [N5-R2]. The evidence base is promising but incomplete: mechanistic evidence is strong, farmworker-specific human evidence is limited, and exposure assessment remains a major limitation [N3-F3], [N5-R3]. Therefore, while the evidence supports a plausible causal pathway, it should be interpreted cautiously and not overgeneralized to all farmworker populations or all agrochemicals.
